title: Does Being Kind Actually Make You Happier?
metaTitle: Does Being Kind Actually Make You Happier?
metaDescription: Yes, modestly and reliably. Research finds acts of kindness give the giver a small-to-moderate wellbeing boost, with spending on others beating self-spending.
keyFinding: Performing acts of kindness gives the helper a small-to-moderate, fairly reliable boost in wellbeing, with the largest effects from varied, freely chosen, in-person kindness — making it one of the lower-cost, better-supported happiness practices available.
honestAnswer: Yes — modestly and fairly reliably. Across the research, doing kind things for others tends to give the helper a small-to-moderate lift in wellbeing, and the effect is consistent enough to take seriously. It is not a dramatic, life-changing intervention, but as happiness practices go it is unusually well supported and unusually cheap.

The realistic framing matters: the boost is modest, it's larger when kindness is varied, freely chosen, and in person, and it can fade when it becomes a rote chore. Kindness also strengthens social bonds, which is itself an indirect route to wellbeing. So the honest answer is yes, with sensible expectations — a reliable small win, not a cure-all.
whatDataShows: A meta-analysis by Curry and colleagues (2018) pulled together experimental studies on performing acts of kindness and found that doing kind things produced a small-to-moderate increase in the wellbeing of the person doing them. Because it synthesises many studies rather than relying on a single result, it's one of the more dependable pieces of evidence in this area.

A well-known set of experiments by Dunn, Aknin and Norton (2008, Science) looked specifically at money. People who were directed to spend on others — 'prosocial spending' — reported greater happiness afterward than those directed to spend the same amount on themselves. The amounts involved were small, suggesting the lift comes from the act of giving rather than the sum.

Research on volunteering points the same direction, with the caveat that much of it is correlational and the effects are modest. Regular volunteering is associated with higher wellbeing, though causation is harder to pin down and the benefit appears strongest when the helping is genuinely chosen rather than obligatory. The kindness benefit looks larger when acts are varied, voluntary, and in person, and smaller when they become repetitive routine.
whyItFeelsDifferent: Kindness can feel like it 'shouldn't' benefit you, because we tend to frame generosity and self-interest as opposites. The idea that helping others also helps you can sound suspiciously convenient — but the research suggests both can be true at once, and that doesn't make the kindness less genuine.

It can also feel underwhelming relative to the cultural promise. Self-help framing sometimes oversells kindness as transformative, so when the real effect turns out to be a modest, quiet lift, it can feel like it 'didn't work.' Calibrated against the evidence, a small reliable boost is actually a good result.

And the benefit erodes when kindness becomes a box to tick. Because freely chosen, varied kindness helps more than rote repetition, turning it into a rigid daily quota can drain the very quality that makes it work. The feeling that it stopped helping is often a sign it became a chore, not that the underlying effect is fake.
whatResearchSaysToDo: Keep it varied and freely chosen. The evidence suggests kindness lifts wellbeing more when the acts differ from day to day and feel genuinely voluntary rather than obligatory. Rotating what you do — and choosing it yourself — preserves the effect better than repeating the same gesture mechanically.

Favour in-person and relational kindness where you can. Acts that involve real contact and connection appear to deliver more, partly because they also strengthen social bonds — and strong relationships are among the most robust predictors of wellbeing. Kindness that builds a relationship works on two channels at once.

When spending, consider directing some of it toward others. Prosocial spending research suggests that using even small amounts on other people tends to lift happiness more than spending the same on yourself. It's a low-cost, well-supported practice — just hold realistic expectations: a modest, reliable win, not a transformation.
whatDoesNotHelp: Treating kindness as a guaranteed mood fix sets you up for disappointment. The effect is real but modest, and overselling it as transformative — as some self-help framing does — invites the conclusion that it 'failed' when it simply did what the evidence predicts: a small, steady lift.

Rote, obligatory kindness delivers less. When acts become a rigid daily quota or a duty rather than a choice, the benefit tends to fade. The research consistently finds freely chosen, varied kindness more effective than mechanical repetition, so grinding through a checklist undercuts the point.

Kindness done mainly for recognition or as a transaction is a weaker route. The wellbeing lift appears tied to genuinely caring about the other person's benefit; performing kindness primarily to be seen, or expecting something specific in return, is not the version the studies show working best.
realNumbersInContext: The size of the effect is the part most worth internalising. Curry and colleagues' 2018 meta-analysis found acts of kindness produced a small-to-moderate boost in the giver's wellbeing — meaningful and fairly reliable, but not large. This is a genuine, low-cost practice, not a dramatic intervention, and calibrating to that scale keeps expectations honest.

On the money side, Dunn, Aknin and Norton (2008) found that spending on others beat spending on oneself for happiness, even at small amounts — pointing to the act of giving rather than the sum as what matters. Volunteering research points the same way but is largely correlational and modest. Taken together: kindness reliably helps a little, helps more when varied, voluntary, and in person, and can fade when it turns into a chore.

faqs.question: Does being kind really make you happier?
faqs.answer: Yes, modestly and fairly reliably. A 2018 meta-analysis (Curry and colleagues) found that performing acts of kindness gives the helper a small-to-moderate boost in wellbeing. It's one of the better-supported, lower-cost happiness practices — just expect a steady small lift rather than a dramatic change.

faqs.question: Is it better to spend money on others or on yourself?
faqs.answer: For happiness, the research leans toward others. Dunn, Aknin and Norton (2008, Science) found people who spent on others reported more happiness than those who spent the same amount on themselves, even with small sums — suggesting the lift comes from the act of giving, not the amount.

faqs.question: Why does kindness sometimes stop feeling good?
faqs.answer: Because the benefit is largest when kindness is varied and freely chosen, and it tends to fade when it becomes rote or obligatory. If it's started to feel flat, that's usually a sign it's become a chore or a fixed routine — rotating what you do and keeping it voluntary helps restore the effect.

faqs.question: Does volunteering make you happier?
faqs.answer: Volunteering is associated with higher wellbeing, and regular volunteers tend to report more of it. The caveat is that much of this research is correlational, so causation is harder to prove, and the benefit appears strongest when the helping is genuinely chosen rather than felt as an obligation.

faqs.question: How big is the effect, realistically?
faqs.answer: Modest. The meta-analytic estimate is a small-to-moderate boost — real and reasonably reliable, but not transformative. The honest way to use this is as a cheap, dependable contributor to wellbeing that also strengthens relationships, not as a single practice that will overhaul how you feel.

dataSources: Curry, O. S., et al. (2018). Happy to help? A systematic review and meta-analysis of the effects of performing acts of kindness on the wellbeing of the actor. Journal of Experimental Social Psychology, 76, 320–329.
